questions.prompt: Why can a single macrophage receptor bind antibodies that recognize thousands of different antigens?

options.text: It binds the variable region, which is the same in all antibodies
Each macrophage makes thousands of different receptor types
Macrophages make the antibodies themselves and keep one copy
It binds the constant region, which is the same across a class

questions.explanation: Like a wall outlet that doesn't care which appliance is plugged in.

options.text: Agglutination
Antibody-dependent cytotoxicity
Opsonization
Neutralization

questions.explanation: Blocking the toxin's active site or a pathogen's attachment works immediately.

Agglutination

questions.prompt: Why can't IgG trigger mast cells to release histamine?

options.text: IgG can't bind any antigens once it leaves B cells
IgG has no variable region to bind the antigen

questions.explanation: Class is set by the constant region, which determines which receptors it fits.

questions.prompt: Which statement about antibody classes is FALSE?

options.text: IgA is the most abundant serum antibody.
IgE sits on the surface of mast cells.
IgM is secreted as a pentamer.
IgG makes up about 80% of serum antibody.

questions.explanation: IgG is most abundant in serum; IgA dominates mucus.

Finches were found to carry antibodies that matched their beak shapes exactly
Antigens change their shape to fit receptors, just as beaks changed for food

questions.prompt: Draw (describe) the primary vs secondary antibody response graph and explain the difference.
questions.explanation: Y = antibody titer, X = time. Primary: ~1-week lag, IgM rises first then IgG, then titers fall — the person usually gets sick. Secondary: memory cells respond immediately; IgM similar but IgG much higher and longer-lasting — usually no disease.

questions.prompt: Give an example of each: natural active, natural passive, artificial active, artificial passive immunity.
questions.explanation: Natural active: getting infected and recovering. Natural passive: IgG across the placenta or IgA in breast milk. Artificial active: a vaccine. Artificial passive: injected antivenom or monoclonal antibodies.
